subject: lighthouse
pitch: A cozy lighthouse diorama on a tiny rocky island. A red-and-white striped tower with a glowing lantern room and a black iron balcony, a keeper's cottage with a crooked chimney and a blue door, a wooden jetty with a rowboat tied to it, a couple of seagulls, tufts of grass and wildflowers between the rocks, and turquoise water with white foam around the shore, all on a round display base.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module built with the SDK, designing a coastal diorama scene on a round base around 1.2 meters across—with a rocky island, tower, cottage, jetty, boat, gulls, grass, flowers, and water, all laid out carefully to avoid runtime errors.

I'm mapping out the SDK's core building blocks I'll need: joints for the skeleton structure, part/lathe/extrude/sweep primitives for geometry, paint options like mottle and stripes for texturing, and cards with SVG textures for grass tufts and wildflowers.

The most robust path forward is leaning on plain three.js geometries through b.part for most shapes, applying Paint objects as colors where baking into a texture sheet makes sense, and using surface scatter plus stick for placing scattered details like foliage. I'm also noting that seagulls would need a simple rig unlike the rest of the static diorama.

Since props don't require explicit joints, I'm defaulting everything to the root joint for simplicity -- one root plus a couple extra joints only if the gulls need independent positioning. For the base, I'm sketching a lathe profile that revolves around the y-axis to form a disc, making sure the lowest point sits exactly at y=0.

Still refining the base and water lathe profiles...

I'm sketching the rocky island bump with a jagged lathe outline, adding mottled grey boulder spheres embedded partway into the surface, and designing a tapered striped tower using a red-and-white banded paint pattern along the height axis.

Now I'm working out the lighthouse top: a glowing yellow glass lantern room, a red conical roof, and a black iron balcony ring, all positioned as stacked lathe profiles above the tower.

For the balcony railing, I'm deciding to loop manually and place thin cylindrical posts at computed positions around the ring rather than using the ring helper, since that gives more direct control over position and orientation.

Now I'm sketching the cottage structure: a box body placed near the island edge, with the roof approximated using a 4-sided cone rotated 45 degrees to look like a pyramid shape, though I'm also considering extruding a proper triangular roof instead.

Right, so the triangular prism extruded along x works: the triangle cross-section in the z-y plane gives sloped roof faces along y-z, with the triangular gable ends sitting on the ±x sides. That gives a proper pitched-roof look.

I'm settling on a red-brown tile roof color, placing a slightly crooked chimney with a tilted rotation, adding a blue front door positioned on the +z face with calculated height centering, and planning small window boxes with white frames and warmish glass tones.

Working out the body shape as a cream-colored box, I'm adjusting the island's lathe profile so the cottage and tower sit embedded naturally into the terrain at the right heights, then starting to plan a wooden jetty extending from the island's edge out toward the water.

I'm now placing the jetty planks and support posts—figuring out plank dimensions, spacing, and grain texture for the deck, plus small cylinder posts anchoring it into the water below.

Next I'm sketching a floating rowboat tied to the jetty, trying out shapes for a tapered hull using a stretched hexagonal cylinder as a simple approximation.

Adding inner hull plate and seat boxes...

I'm thinking about adding a rope from boat to jetty post using a thin rod connector, and considering a foam ring effect near the shore using a closed lathe profile offset from the axis.

For the island base and water disc, I'm checking radii so the foam ring sits just outside the rock edge rather than hidden inside it, then setting the water surface to a turquoise mottled color with a lathe disc slightly smaller than the island base radius.

The water disc intersects the island so it rises visibly out of the surface — since the water top is solid and at a lower height than the island's upper portion, the island will appear to poke through naturally, giving the look of land emerging from the sea.

For vegetation, I'm planning grass blades and wildflowers as textured cards placed on surface frames pointing upward, sized small and scattered across the island's visible ring while avoiding the tower, cottage, and jetty footprints. I'll need a height function or surface-based scatter to place them realistically on the island's sloped profile rather than guessing flat coordinates.

For textures I'm planning svg-based card textures for flowers and additional scattered boulders using separate rng seeds. I'm now sketching a simple seagull model built from a capsule body, sphere head, cone beak, and slab wings positioned at flight height.

For the beak, I'm working out the right rotation so the cone tip points forward along z. For the wings, I'm extruding a flattened outline in the x-z plane to get a horizontal spread, then mirroring the point set to create a matching left and right wing.

For positioning each gull, I'm considering using a joint as a pivot so the parts attach rigidly in world space and inherit the joint's orientation, which seems cleaner than manually computing rotated positions for each part.

I'm placing the two gulls off to the side near the tower so nothing hangs directly above it, keeping their positions in flight rather than perched. Then I'm checking part/triangle counts stay reasonable before moving to the balcony's iron ring railing, sizing it against the tower radius at that height.

Working out the lantern room assembly now: a balcony floor ring sitting just below the tower top, a glass lantern housing with mullions above it, a pointed red roof lathe, and a ball finial on top. I'm sketching the railing posts and top rail dimensions to fit the balcony radius.

Then I'm turning to the tower's painted stripe pattern, verifying the paint axis mapping works correctly on the lathed surface, and planning the cottage facade details — door centered on the front wall with two small framed windows flanking it.

Next I'm sketching the gabled roof as an extrusion sitting atop the cottage walls, making sure the roof overhang clears the wall boundaries on both sides and the triangular gable ends align properly with the wall faces.

Then I'm adding a crooked brick chimney positioned where it pierces the roof slope correctly, tilting it slightly for a rustic look and checking that its base stays embedded within the roof geometry while the cap sits above the roofline.

For visual charm I'm placing small white smoke puffs floating above the chimney at increasing heights, plus scattering low-poly dodecahedron boulders across the island terrain, estimating the ground height at each radius so the rocks sit naturally embedded rather than floating.

I'm working out the island's cross-sectional profile and checking that the tower and cottage bases sit flush against the terrain rather than poking through or floating above it, then extending a wooden jetty out from the island's edge over the water, positioning deck planks and support posts so the deck surface stays just above the waterline.

I realize the boat I'm placing near the jetty is too long and pokes outside the island's base radius, so I'm repositioning it closer to the island edge and considering shrinking its length so it fits within the scene bounds.

I'm now recalculating the deck's position and dimensions so its corners stay within the base radius while still aligning sensibly with the island and post placement.

Checking the boat's position against the island edge — its bow at x 0.52 and the rope tying it to the post seem fine, but the hull itself might overlap the island's rim near radius 0.42, so I need to shift the boat further out into clear water.

To fix this, I'm shrinking the island's base radius to about 0.33-0.34 and reworking its profile curve, then widening the foam ring to r 0.36-0.46 so the boat at roughly (0.42, 0.28) sits cleanly outside the island boundary.

I'm overthinking the foam/boat overlap near the rock edge, so instead I'll just relocate the boat to the opposite side, maybe near where a jetty might go, to sidestep the collision entirely.

Checking the cottage placement — its corners slightly overhang the island edge, so I'm nudging it inward to around (0.14, 0.12) to keep clear of both the water boundary and the tower's footprint.

Working through the roof overhang, door placement, and a small step leading up to it, making sure each piece lines up with the body box and sits properly above the island surface without clipping below it.

Now I'm positioning the two windows symmetrically on the front face, checking that their spans don't overlap the door, and figuring out the roof height along the ridge to place a chimney—computing the slope's height falloff near the back edge to see where the chimney should sit on the back-facing slope.

I'm sizing the chimney box and cap, angling them to match the roof pitch, then scattering small spheres above it as smoke puffs. Setting up the texture choices (stripes for the tower, mottled textures for water and rock, grain for the deck), then starting the module imports and scaffolding for the build script.

Writing the lighthouse builder function...

Still shaping island mesh and foam ring geometry...

Confirming the tower base sits embedded in the island correctly, then I'm adding the lantern room as a yellow glass lathe shape on top, with black mullion boxes spaced around it at angular intervals to create a window-frame effect.

Now I'm building the lantern roof as a red tapering lathe shape with a small spherical finial, plus a dark balcony floor platform, and defining shared tower position offsets. I'm placing railing posts in a circle around the balcony with a torus-shaped top rail, then starting on a cream-colored cottage body box positioned off to the side.

For the cottage I'm extruding a triangular roof profile in a brick-red color, adding a tilted chimney with a cap, and placing a blue front door with a white frame slightly offset for depth.

For the windows, I'm positioning paired frame-and-glass boxes with pale yellow panes along the facade, plus a small flower box beneath each sill for added detail.

Now I'm sketching out the seagulls — small capsule-shaped bodies attached to joints, so I can position each bird at a fixed spot near the roof with proper bone binding for articulation.

Still defining the head, beak, and wings for each gull, using extruded outline shapes in the x-z plane to give the wings a tapered, swept-back look.

Since the base joint has no children, its bone collapses to a point, so nearest-joint lookup just defaults back to the base — that's fine for the gull setup, skipping the wing role concern. Now I'm placing scattered rocks using small dodecahedron geometries in a mottled grey, positioning them along the island's surface curve near the edge.

I'm figuring out rock placements by checking their radial distance and height against the island's lathe profile, nudging coordinates so they sit just outside the deck and tower zones. Then I'm setting up a scatter function for grass and flowers across the island surface, filtering out points near the tower, cottage, and jetty footprints, and restricting to upward-facing points so nothing ends up planted on the steep sides.

I'm separating grass and flowers into two scatter passes with different densities and seeds, then rendering them as textured cards with randomized lean, bend, and spin for a natural look. Writing SVG grass texture...

Now I'm designing the flower SVG with a stem anchored at the bottom (so the card's root aligns correctly) and petals arranged around a yellow center, planning to vary petal colors across instances for diversity.

I'm also sketching the boat geometry—extruded hull outline with a pointed bow, placed with its thickness along the vertical axis—and considering whether to add painted stripes along the hull for detail, plus foam rings around the shore and smoke puff spheres for the scene.

Inside the boat, I'm planning a wooden floor plank, interior gunwale trim in red, oars resting as simple wood-colored rods, and a rope connecting a deck post to the bow. For the jetty, I'm adding a painted deck box and considering darker plank lines across it for texture.

Now I'm working through the remaining structural pieces: cylindrical posts for the jetty, double-checking that deck and post heights align properly, and confirming the island's boulders and flower boxes are accounted for. I'm skipping a brass plaque idea on the base as unnecessary, and reviewing builder setup details like paint size, texture functions (grain, stripes, mottle), and part defaults to make sure everything will render correctly before returning the final root object.

Checking the grass card scatter logic, I confirm hits carry proper surface normals, cards attach correctly to the island's base joint for skinning weights, and triangle/mesh counts stay reasonable across island segments and card instances. I also verify the keepOut callback type doesn't need a THREE import since it's just a boolean predicate on a position.

Now I'm reviewing required fields like `at` for lathe, extrude, joints, and part options, making sure every call supplies the needed position and color parameters before drafting the actual lighthouse diorama code.

I'm working through the remaining details—beak orientation, wing extrusions, gull placement to avoid overlap with the tower, and verifying joint parenting logic resolves correctly since each gull attaches to the base. I'm also double-checking that all imports (stripes, mottle, grain, rng) are used correctly, that lathe and extrude closing points align properly, and that part counts and shadow requirements are reasonable before finalizing the mullion and railing post loops.
